motion: The iPhone 17 Pro Max takes better portraits than the Samsung S26 Ultra

rounds.text: Portrait mode is about the subject, and Samsung gives you more to work with. The 3x telephoto lets you stand further back, which flattens faces naturally, and the higher resolution means you can crop without losing detail. Skin texture is sharper too. The iPhone's softer look hides detail many people actually want.

Sharper is not better for faces. Samsung's processing over-sharpens skin and makes pores look harsh, which is why so many Samsung portraits get edited afterwards. The iPhone's depth mapping is also more accurate: hair, glasses and ear edges are cut out cleanly. A portrait you don't need to fix is a better portrait.

Edge detection has caught up. In side-by-side tests posted in this very thread, Samsung handled hair well in daylight. And processing is a setting: Samsung lets you turn down sharpening. The iPhone gives you one look and no control. For people who like to choose their style, that matters.

Most people never open settings. They point, shoot and post. Judge what the phone produces by default, and the iPhone's defaults are more natural. The skin tones are also more consistent across different complexions, which matters a lot in India, where Samsung often brightens darker skin too much.

Defaults matter, but so does the camera hardware. Samsung's zoom gives you more framing options at a wedding or event, where you can't always step closer. Better hardware plus adjustable processing beats a pleasant default.

Framing options don't help if the result looks processed. Natural skin tones, clean edges and a photo you can post without editing: that is what makes a better portrait for most people. The iPhone delivers that every time.
